title: The Apology of Socrates, Plato
subtitle: 399 BC AD
subject: litterature
description: In 399 BC, Athens tried Socrates. Accused of corrupting youth, he refuses to plead for mercy. Plato sets the founding scene of Western philosophy.

hero.hook: A public trial. A man who would rather die than remain silent.

blocks.text: In **399 BC**, in Athens, **Socrates**, son of a sculptor and a midwife, was put on trial. He is accused of not honoring the gods of the city and of **corrupting the youth**, that is to say of inciting them to question the authorities. The **Apology**, written by his disciple **Plato**, is not an apology. In Greek,  means “defense”. [[apologia]]

Socrates does not play the repentant accused. He transforms the tribunal into an examination of the city. The verdict will be death by **hemlock**, a toxic plant. The scene will become a founding myth of Western thought.

Athens is emerging from wars and political crises. The defeat against Sparta in 404 still weighs heavily. Socrates questions the powerful in the public square. He unmasks those who think they know without having verified. For some, it's piety. For others, it's subversion. The [[sophists]], paid professors of rhetoric, are also in the landscape. Socrates stands out from them, but public opinion sometimes confuses them.

blocks.caption: The trial of Socrates: Athenian democracy judges its spoilsport.

blocks.text: The trial mixes religion and politics. We don't just judge abstract ideas. We judge a lifestyle that is disturbing: a man who spends his days asking questions, without official function, without remaining silent in front of the powerful.

The oracle says: no one is wiser than him. He then understands that his wisdom is**negative**. The others think they know. He knows that he doesn't know. Hence the famous formula: . [[“I know I don’t know anything”]]
His method, , compares dialogue to childbirth: creating clearer thoughts in others, through successive questions, without imposing a ready-made lesson. [[Socratic maieutics]]
In court, this posture irritates. Instead of begging, Socrates explains why an unexamined **life** is not worth defending. He prefers death to betrayal of his mission.

Found guilty, Socrates must propose an alternative punishment to death. Instead of careful exile, he suggests being fed at the [[Prytaneum]], a public building in Athens where the city honored its benefactors. This is a calculated provocation. The judges vote for death.

blocks.caption: The Death of Socrates, by David: the calm of the philosopher in the face of hemlock.

blocks.text: He refuses to flee later, in the dialogue **Crito**, another text by Plato. Obeying laws in form, while criticizing them in substance: the Socratic paradox begins here. Socrates accepts the sentence to remain consistent with his entire life.

Plato makes this death the baptism of philosophy. Thinking can be expensive. The Apology inspires the Stoics, the Christians, the **Lights** of the 18th century, the modern resistance fighters. It fixes an image: the wise man who prefers the truth to comfortable survival.

This account is not a neutral account. Plato chooses what to remember: an attitude, not just arguments. After Socrates, philosophizing also means accepting that the truth can be costly in the city. The Apology remains the first great text where thought defends itself against power.
The **Apology of Socrates** shows a man who refuses to beg for his life. In **399**, Athens kills a troublesome citizen and invents, despite itself, the martyr of free thought.
